specPoints.text: be able to draw the reaction profiles for uncatalysed and catalysed reactions, including the energy level of the intermediate formed with the catalyst

primer.text: Catalysts cheat by geography, not by magic: they open a second route whose energy hill is lower. This note sorts homogeneous from heterogeneous catalysis, draws both the profile humps and the shaded distribution areas, and totals the industrial prizes of speed, cost and atom economy.

lessons.title: Catalysis: the lower pathway and its three prizes
lessons.opening: A catalyst is not a shortcut magic - it is an alternative route with a lower activation hill. Industry prizes it for speed, for cooler cheaper plants, and for atom economy gains like zeolite-catalysed phenol synthesis.
keyPoints: Catalysis increases reaction rate by providing an alternative pathway of lower activation energy.
Three advantages: more product per unit time, lower energy costs, and potentially better atom economy.
Zeolites in phenol synthesis show how a catalyst can suppress unwanted side products.
The catalyst is unchanged at the end, ready to work again.

low.restatement: The catalysed route crosses a smaller energy hill, so more collisions succeed per second; the same reactants and products emerge, only faster and cheaper.
low.analogy: A mountain pass rerouted through a lower col: the destination is identical, the climb is easier, so more travellers arrive per hour.
low.examPointer: On profiles, draw TWO humps sharing reactant and product levels, the catalysed hump lower, and label both Ea values.

medium.restatement: Lowering Ea enlarges the fraction of collisions that clear the barrier; nothing about collision frequency changes. Industrial wins follow: lower temperature bills, higher throughput, and fewer side reactions trimming waste.
medium.analogy: Lowering a hurdle on a racecourse does not add runners; it just lets more of the same runners clear it.
medium.examPointer: Quote all three advantages when a question says 'state the benefits of industrial catalysis' - speed, cost, atom economy.

options.text: Providing an alternative reaction pathway with lower activation energy
options.explanation: The lowered barrier lets a greater proportion of collisions succeed.

options.text: Raising the collision energy of the reactants
options.explanation: Collision energies depend on temperature; the catalyst does not heat the mixture.

options.text: Increasing the collision frequency directly
options.explanation: Frequency rises only via temperature, concentration or pressure changes.

options.text: Shifting the equilibrium position
options.explanation: Catalysts speed both directions equally; position is untouched.

check.stem: Which is NOT one of the three main advantages of industrial catalysts?

options.text: They increase the activation energy of side reactions to zero
options.explanation: No advantage involves zero Ea; the trio is rate, cost, atom economy.

options.text: They allow lower temperatures and pressures, cutting energy costs
options.explanation: This is the cost advantage of the trio.

options.text: They can improve atom economy by suppressing side reactions
options.explanation: Zeolites in phenol synthesis exemplify this.

options.text: They raise the rate, making more product per unit time
options.explanation: This is the speed advantage of the trio.

check.stem: Zeolites in phenol synthesis demonstrate that catalysts can

options.text: Reduce the amount of unwanted side products
options.explanation: The alternative pathway favours the wanted product, trimming waste.

options.text: Change the identity of the final product
options.explanation: The same products form; only the route and speed differ.

options.text: Raise the overall activation energy
options.explanation: Catalysts lower, never raise, the barrier.

options.text: Be consumed stoichiometrically
options.explanation: Catalysts are regenerated, not consumed.

check.stem: On an energy profile, the catalysed pathway is drawn as

options.text: A second hump from the same reactants to the same products, with a lower maximum
options.explanation: Both routes share endpoints; the catalysed maximum is lower.

options.text: A straight horizontal line
options.explanation: Reactions still need some barrier to cross.

options.text: A deeper hump than the uncatalysed one
options.explanation: Deeper (higher) would mean slower.

options.text: A route to different products entirely
options.explanation: The products are unchanged by catalysis.

check.stem: Lower energy costs follow from catalysis because

options.text: The reaction proceeds adequately at lower temperatures and pressures
options.explanation: The lowered barrier compensates for milder conditions.

options.text: The catalyst generates free energy
options.explanation: No catalyst creates energy; thermodynamics is untouched.

options.text: Fuels are unnecessary in catalysed plants
options.explanation: Heating still occurs, just less of it.

options.text: The catalyst absorbs the enthalpy change
options.explanation: The enthalpy change of reaction is a property of the reaction itself.

check.modelAnswer: The process of increasing reaction rate by adding a catalyst that provides an alternative pathway of lower activation energy.

check.stem: State the three main advantages of using catalysts industrially.
check.modelAnswer: Higher rate and so more product per unit time; lower energy costs from milder conditions; potentially improved atom economy with fewer side products.

check.stem: Explain why a catalyst is not consumed overall in a reaction it speeds up.
check.modelAnswer: The catalyst participates in the alternative mechanism but is regenerated in a later step, so its amount after the reaction equals its amount before.

check.stem: A plant switches to a zeolite catalyst and cuts its reactor temperature by 80 oC with no yield loss. State the two economic gains.
check.modelAnswer: Lower fuel bills from the milder temperature, and maintained (often improved) throughput and atom economy since the catalysed pathway suppresses side products.

lessons.title: Homogeneous and heterogeneous catalysts on the curve
lessons.opening: Catalysts come in two phases of life: homogeneous, sharing the reactants' phase, and heterogeneous, standing apart as the industrial standard. On the energy curve, either kind drags the Ea line leftward and the shaded success area balloons.
keyPoints: Homogeneous catalysts share the same physical phase as the reactants, typically all in solution.
Heterogeneous catalysts sit in a different phase from the reactants, most commonly a solid with gaseous reactants.
Heterogeneous catalysis is the most common type in industry.
Lowering Ea means a greater proportion of molecules possess sufficient energy for effective collisions, enlarging the shaded success area.

low.restatement: Same-phase catalysts mingle with reactants molecule by molecule; different-phase catalysts work at their surfaces. Both shrink the energy hurdle, so the beyond-Ea area grows and the rate climbs.
low.analogy: A dance teacher on the floor (homogeneous) versus a climbing wall fixed at the side (heterogeneous) - both help dancers reach the high shelf faster.
low.examPointer: Classify industrial examples correctly: solid iron in ammonia synthesis is heterogeneous; aqueous catalysts with aqueous reactants are homogeneous.

medium.restatement: Phase matching determines the contact mode - bulk collisions versus surface adsorption - but the kinetic effect is identical: reduced Ea, enlarged tail area, faster rate. Industry favours heterogeneous systems for easy separation and reuse.
medium.analogy: A filter that works mid-stream versus one bolted to the pipe wall: different contact, same lowered resistance to flow.
medium.examPointer: On the curve, the catalysed Ea line sits left of the uncatalysed line; the combined light-and-dark shaded areas show the new reactive population.

check.stem: A homogeneous catalyst is one that is

options.text: In the same physical phase as the reactants
options.explanation: Homogeneous means phase-matched, such as everything in solution.

options.text: Always a solid metal surface
options.explanation: That describes heterogeneous catalysis.

options.text: Chemically identical to the reactants
options.explanation: Phase, not chemical identity, defines the term.

options.text: Effective only in the gas phase
options.explanation: Homogeneous catalysis commonly runs in solution.

check.stem: The most common industrial catalyst type is

options.text: Heterogeneous, typically a solid with gaseous reactants
options.explanation: Solid beds with gas streams dominate industrial plants.

options.text: Homogeneous, all dissolved together
options.explanation: Solution catalysis is common in labs, less in industry.

options.text: Biological enzymes exclusively
options.explanation: Enzymes are one family, not the industrial standard.

options.text: Undefined, as catalysts have no phases
options.explanation: Phases are exactly what the classification uses.

check.stem: On the Maxwell-Boltzmann curve, adding a catalyst

options.text: Moves the Ea line left, enlarging the shaded area of effective molecules
options.explanation: The lowered barrier admits a larger fraction of the same population.

options.text: Reshapes the curve into a taller peak
options.explanation: The distribution shape depends on temperature only.

options.text: Reduces the total area under the curve
options.explanation: The molecule count is conserved.

options.text: Shifts the whole curve to the right
options.explanation: That is heating's signature, not catalysis.

check.stem: Heterogeneous catalysts suit industry partly because

options.text: A solid catalyst is easily separated from gaseous or liquid product streams
options.explanation: Phase difference makes recovery and reuse straightforward.

options.text: They dissolve completely into the reactants
options.explanation: Dissolving would make separation harder, and that is homogeneous behaviour.

options.text: They require no reactor vessel
options.explanation: Solid beds live inside reactors.

options.text: They eliminate all side reactions
options.explanation: They reduce some, not all.

check.stem: A gas-phase reactant mixture over an iron surface is an example of

options.text: Heterogeneous catalysis
options.explanation: Gas reactants with a solid catalyst sit in different phases.

options.text: Homogeneous catalysis
options.explanation: The phases differ, so the term cannot apply.

options.text: No catalysis
options.explanation: Iron surfaces catalyse gas reactions industrially.

options.text: Enzyme catalysis
options.explanation: Iron is not an enzyme.

check.modelAnswer: A catalyst in a different physical phase from the reactants, most often a solid surface with gaseous or dissolved reactants.

check.stem: State what the combined light and dark shaded areas represent on the catalysis curve.
check.modelAnswer: The number of molecules with energy greater than the catalysed activation energy, which is far larger than the dark area alone for the uncatalysed barrier.

check.stem: Explain why the rate of the catalysed reaction exceeds the uncatalysed rate.
check.modelAnswer: The alternative pathway's lower Ea admits a greater proportion of the unchanged energy distribution into effective collision, so more successful collisions occur per unit time.

check.stem: A chemist dissolves both reactant and catalyst in water. Classify the system and predict the effect on Ea.
check.modelAnswer: Homogeneous catalysis, since everything shares the aqueous phase; the catalyst lowers the activation energy by providing an alternative pathway, raising the rate.

glossary.definition: A substance providing an alternative reaction pathway of lower activation energy, unchanged at the reaction's end.
A catalyst in the same physical phase as its reactants, such as an aqueous catalyst with aqueous reactants.
A catalyst in a different phase from the reactants, typically a solid bed serving a gas stream; the common industrial type.
